```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# The workflow code is read from the companion script and shown, not run.
# Results come from the cache that script writes.
knitr::read_chunk(file.path("..", "scripts", "05-io-yft-ss3-to-opal-workflow.r"))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE)
options(knitr.kable.NA = "—")
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)

cache = readRDS(file.path("data", "io-yft-workflow-cache.rds"))
C  = cache$convergence
S  = cache$summary
B  = cache$bridge

col = c("SS3" = "grey20", "opal" = "#1E8449",
        "opal at SS3 values" = "#C0392B", "replay with SS3 timing" = "#2471A3",
        "observed" = "grey55")
scale_series = list(scale_colour_manual(values = col, name = NULL))
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
          theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank()))

fleet_name = function(f) {
    f  = as.integer(f)
    nm = c(cache$fleet_names[1:16], paste0("llcpue_q", 1:4))
    lv = sprintf("%d: %s", seq_along(nm), nm)
    factor(lv[f], levels = lv)
}
fmt = function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
sci = function(x, d = 1) formatC(x, format = "e", digits = d)
pct = function(x, d = 1) paste0(fmt(100 * x, d), "%")
```

# Purpose

This guide shows how a Stock Synthesis 3 (SS3) assessment is converted into
an [opal](https://github.com/N-DucharmeBarth-NOAA/opal) model, how to test
that the conversion is right, and how to set up and fit the opal model. It
works through one example from start to finish: the IATTC team's SS3 model of
the Indian Ocean yellowfin (IO YFT) simulated data, which became opal fit
**C2**. It is written for analysts converting their own SS3 model, and
section 9 lists what to compare between your model and this one.

All the code is in one companion script,
`case-studies/io-yft/scripts/05-io-yft-ss3-to-opal-workflow.r`. The code shown below is
taken from that script, not retyped. Copy the script and edit it for your
model. The results here are from the script's own run, read from the cache
it writes.

This guide covers the workflow only. For how the opal fits compare with SS3
and with the simulated truth, and why they differ, see:

* `ss3-to-opal-io-yft.qmd`: the first conversion, with both biology routes,
  diagnostic fits and the comparison with the operating model.
* `ss3-to-opal-io-yft-age-k.qmd`: SS3's age-specific K growth in opal, and
  the selectivity fits C and C2.
* `simulations/sims-synthesis.qmd`: simulations of the catch-timing and
  selectivity differences between the two platforms.

## How the converter works

The converter is a set of R functions in `shared/ss3-to-opal/`:

| File | What it does |
|---|---|
| `ss3-read.R` | Reads the SS3 files with r4ss and records their checksums |
| `ss3-convert.R` | Converts dimensions, fleets, catch, indices, length compositions, selectivity and parameters (`ss3_to_opal()`) |
| `ss3-biology.R` | Converts biology and growth: M, weight, maturity, spawning potential, length-at-age |
| `ss3-validate.R` | Tests: structural checks, reconciliation with SS3, the bridging replay |
| `ss3-opal-obj.R` | Builds the opal object and switches selectivity between SS3's and opal's |
| `ss3-fit-tools.R` | Newton polishing after `nlminb`, and extraction helpers |

The converter follows three rules:

1. **Derived quantities come from `Report.sso`** wherever SS3 reports them:
   M, weight, maturity and spawning potential at age, selectivity at age,
   unfished spawning biomass and the recruitment bias ramp. These quantities
   already include every transformation SS3 applied internally, so nothing
   has to be re-derived from the control file.
2. **Every decision that cannot be read from the SS3 files is in one settings
   list.** That includes how to split an index, which fleets' compositions to
   use and which opal curve to use for each fleet. The functions hard-code
   nothing about the model.
3. **Where opal cannot represent SS3 exactly, the converter reports how close
   it gets** rather than hiding the approximation.

The workflow has eight steps:

| Step | Section | Main functions | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Settings | 3 | an R list | `cfg` |
| 2. Read SS3 | 4 | `ss3_read_model()` | `ss3` |
| 3. Convert | 5 | `ss3_to_opal()`, `prep_lf_data()` | `converted` |
| 4. Test inputs | 6.1–6.2 | `validate_opal_inputs()`, `ss3_reconcile()` | check tables |
| 5. Build | 6.3 | `ss3_opal_obj()` | `assessment` |
| 6. Test dynamics | 6.4–6.5 | `ss3_use_external_selectivity()`, `ss3_bridge_table()` | bridging table |
| 7. Set up and fit | 7 | `ss3_seed_par_sel()`, `ss3_use_estimated_selectivity()`, `opal_fit()` | `fit` |
| 8. Inspect and save | 7–8 | `opal_report()`, `opal_save()` | results, saved fit |

# What you need

* R with **opal** ≥ 0.1.1 (`dev` branch; 0.1.1 adds SS3's age-specific K
  growth), **r4ss**, **data.table**, **magrittr** and **this.path**.
* The SS3 model folder, with these files from a converged run:
  * `data.ss_new` (data);
  * `control.ss_new` (control);
  * `ss3.par` (parameter estimates; called `ss.par` in some versions);
  * `Report.sso`, which the converter needs for biology, selectivity and B0.
* The converter functions (`shared/ss3-to-opal/`).

# The conversion settings

Everything the converter needs to know beyond the SS3 files is in `cfg`, a
plain R list. The table below lists each block. The values below are for
IO YFT, and each needs to be checked again for another model.

| Block | Decision | IO YFT choice |
|---|---|---|
| `time` | Which SS3 time steps become opal time steps | All 256; each SS3 "year" is a quarter, so opal has `n_year = 256`, `n_season = 1` |
| `age` | Which SS3 ages to keep | 1–28, so the opal age equals the SS3 age (age 0 dropped) |
| `growth` | How opal computes length-at-age | `ss3_age_k`: SS3's `GrowthModel 3` reproduced exactly |
| `bio` | Where M, weight, maturity and spawning potential come from | `endgrowth`: Report.sso's age table, used directly |
| `index` | How SS3's index fleets map to opal index series | Fleet 17 split into four quarterly series (opal 17–20) |
| `lf` | Which fleets' length compositions to use, and the bin grid | Fleets 1–14 and 16; last bin regularised to 195–200 cm |
| `selectivity` | opal curve per fishery, and which parameters to estimate | Double-normal for fisheries, logistic for the index; estimate what SS3 estimated |

```{r settings}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
```

Points that are easy to get wrong:

* **Time units.** opal's time step is the model step. When the SS3 year is a
  quarter, SS3 still reads M and the von Bertalanffy K as *annual* rates and
  applies them over the season. The converter divides both by
  `12 / (nseas × months_per_seas)`, which is 4 here (`bio$m_rate_divisor`).
* **Biology route.** `endgrowth` takes biology at age from SS3 exactly. Use
  `control` only if growth is to be estimated in opal: it rebuilds weight and
  maturity on a length basis and converts them through opal's
  length-at-age, so any difference in growth then reaches spawning biomass.
* **Selectivity codes.** `opal_type_f` uses opal's codes (1 logistic,
  2 double-normal, 3 double Richards), not SS3 pattern numbers.
  `validate_opal_inputs()` checks this.
* **Index splitting** is a modelling choice: one SS3 index with one
  catchability, against four opal series with four. Leave `split` empty to
  keep SS3's index as one series.
* **`estimate`, `mirror`, `free_par` and `fix_prior_dominated`** are used only
  when the final model is set up (section 7), not during conversion.

# Convert

```{r convert}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
```

`ss3_to_opal()` returns:

* `data`: the opal data list;
* `parameters`: starting values at SS3's estimates;
* `lf`: length compositions in long format;
* `selectivity`: SS3's selectivity-at-age, and the same projected onto length
  bins;
* `meta`: diagnostics and provenance;
* `ss3`: the r4ss objects it read.

The starting values are SS3's own estimates:

* `log_B0` is SS3's unfished spawning biomass (opal estimates B0, not R0).
* `rdev_y` holds SS3's recruitment deviations.
* Steepness and σ~R~ come from the par file.
* Growth comes from the SS3 files.
* Each fishery's initial F is set to effectively zero (`log_init_F_f`), so the
  model starts unfished.
* Catchabilities start at 1.

Then `prep_lf_data()` (an opal function) adds the length compositions to the
data list. SS3's `mult_by_lencomp_N` becomes opal's `lf_var_adjust`; opal
divides the sample size by it, so the converter passes the reciprocal.

Two opal rules affect anything you add to the data list:

* **Only plain R objects.** `opal_obj()` rejects data elements that hold an
  external pointer, and every data.table has one. Convert to `data.frame`
  (as above) or run `ss3_make_portable()` on the list.
* **Change an opal object only through `opal_update()`.** The object stores a
  hash of its contents. Assigning directly (`x$data$foo <- ...`) makes the
  next validation fail with "Model state was modified directly". The
  `ss3_use_*()` helpers all go through `opal_update()`.

# Test the conversion

The tests run in order, from the cheapest and most specific to the most
general. A failure at one level should be fixed before moving on, because the
later tests cannot separate a conversion error from a real difference between
the two models.

| Test | Asks | Fails when |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Structure | Is the opal input internally consistent? | dimension mismatches, wrong codes, non-portable objects |
| 2. Reconciliation | Did the data and biology survive the conversion? | lost or duplicated observations, wrong units, wrong female fraction |
| 3. Build | Can opal evaluate the model at the starting values? | non-finite objective or gradient |
| 4. Bridging | At SS3's parameters, does opal reproduce SS3's dynamics? | any remaining conversion error that affects the population |

## Test 1: structure

```{r check-structure}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
```

`validate_opal_inputs()` checks the following:

* dimensions (ages, years, fisheries, length bins);
* that M, weight, maturity and spawning potential have a valid length and
  range;
* catch array shape and units codes;
* index columns, index numbering and time window;
* length composition bins and fisheries;
* parameter vector lengths;
* selectivity codes;
* that nothing non-portable is in the data list.

For IO YFT, **`r sum(cache$checks$pass)` of `r nrow(cache$checks)`** checks
pass.

```{r check-table}
ck = cache$checks[, .(check, pass = ifelse(pass, "yes", "**no**"))]
knitr::kable(ck, col.names = c("Check", "Pass"))
```

## Test 2: reconciliation with SS3

```{r check-reconcile}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
```

`ss3_reconcile()` compares quantities that should match SS3 exactly. Each has
a relative tolerance of 10^-6^, except spawning potential per recruit, which
has 10^-4^. The most informative row is **unfished spawning potential per
recruit**: one number that would show M in the wrong time units (a factor of
about 4 here), a misplaced female fraction (a factor of 2) or a wrong
plus-group treatment. Its small residual comes from two places: Report.sso
prints six significant figures, and SS3 3.24 closes the plus group
differently from opal.

```{r recon-table}
rc = cache$recon[, .(quantity,
                     ss3  = ifelse(is.na(ss3),  NA, formatC(ss3,  format = "g", digits = 7)),
                     opal = ifelse(is.na(opal), NA, formatC(opal, format = "g", digits = 7)),
                     rel_diff = sci(rel_diff, 1),
                     pass = ifelse(is.na(pass), "—", ifelse(pass, "yes", "**no**")))]
knitr::kable(rc, col.names = c("Quantity", "SS3", "opal", "Relative difference", "Pass"),
             align = "lrrrc")
```

The length-at-age row compares opal's growth (`get_growth()` with SS3's
parameters and K multipliers) with SS3's `Len_Beg`. Its error is at the level
of Report.sso's print precision, so the growth conversion is exact. With
`growth$model = "schnute"` this row would report how well a single-k curve
approximates SS3's growth.

## Test 3: build the opal object

```{r build}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
```

`ss3_opal_obj()` does three things:

* attaches opal's default priors (`get_priors()`);
* records the SS3 file checksums, r4ss version and settings in
  `$provenance$metadata`;
* runs `opal_build()`, which builds the RTMB tape and checks that the
  objective and gradient are finite at the starting values.

The default map (`get_map()`) estimates `log_B0`, the recruitment deviations
and the catchabilities, and fixes growth and selectivity.

## Test 4: bridging at SS3's parameters

This is the main test of the conversion. SS3's selectivity-at-age is put into
opal directly (`sel_fa_external`), every parameter is left at SS3's value,
and nothing is estimated. opal's spawning biomass is then compared with
SS3's.

```{r check-bridge}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
```

Even with every input converted exactly, the two models differ in two
places:

* **Catch timing.** opal removes each step's catch at the start of the
  step, before natural mortality. SS3 applies fishing and natural mortality
  together through the Baranov equation.
* **Recruitment timing.** opal recruits the first age class at *t* + 1 from
  spawning biomass at *t* + 1. With SS3 age 0 dropped, SS3's matching fish
  were recruited from spawning biomass at *t*.

`ss3_bridge_replica()` replays the population on the converted inputs, either
with opal's timing or with SS3's:

* With opal's timing it reproduces `opal_report()`.
* With SS3's timing it should reproduce SS3's spawning biomass.

**A small residual under SS3's timing shows that the conversion is correct.**
Any gap left between opal and SS3 is then a real difference between the
platforms, not a conversion error.

```{r bridge-figure}
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Bridging test. Top: spawning biomass from SS3, from opal at SS3's parameter values with SS3's selectivity-at-age, and from the converted inputs replayed with SS3's catch and recruitment timing. Bottom: each relative to SS3."
bl = rbind(B[, .(ts, value = ss3, series = "SS3", panel = "Spawning biomass (t)")],
           B[, .(ts, value = opal, series = "opal at SS3 values", panel = "Spawning biomass (t)")],
           B[, .(ts, value = replica_ss3, series = "replay with SS3 timing", panel = "Spawning biomass (t)")],
           B[, .(ts, value = 100 * rel_opal, series = "opal at SS3 values", panel = "Difference from SS3 (%)")],
           B[, .(ts, value = 100 * rel_replica_ss3, series = "replay with SS3 timing", panel = "Difference from SS3 (%)")])
bl[, panel := factor(panel, levels = c("Spawning biomass (t)", "Difference from SS3 (%)"))]
ggplot(bl, aes(ts, value, colour = series)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
    facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
    scale_series + labs(x = "Time step (quarter)", y = NULL)
```

```{r bridge-table}
bt = data.table(
    series = c("opal at SS3 values", "converted inputs, replayed with SS3 timing"),
    mean_abs = c(mean(abs(B$rel_opal)), mean(abs(B$rel_replica_ss3))),
    max_abs  = c(max(abs(B$rel_opal)), max(abs(B$rel_replica_ss3))))
knitr::kable(bt[, .(series, pct(mean_abs, 2), pct(max_abs, 2))],
             col.names = c("Series", "Mean |difference| from SS3", "Max |difference| from SS3"),
             align = "lrr")
```

For IO YFT, opal at SS3's values differs from SS3 by up to
`r pct(max(abs(B$rel_opal)))`. The replay with SS3's timing differs by at
most `r pct(max(abs(B$rel_replica_ss3)), 2)`. The conversion is therefore
correct, and the opal–SS3 gap at fixed parameters comes from catch timing.
The simulations in `simulations/` measure how much that timing difference
matters in estimation.

If the replay with SS3's timing does *not* match SS3, look for a conversion
error. Common causes:

* catch units (biomass vs numbers) or a fleet out of order;
* M or K not rescaled to the time step;
* a female fraction applied twice or not at all;
* selectivity read for the wrong fleet, year or `Factor` (`Asel` vs
  `Asel2`);
* recruitment deviations misaligned by a step.

The replay needs biology at age and SS3's selectivity, so it works only with
the `endgrowth` route.

## Starting objective and gradient

```{r start-objective}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
```

```{r start-table}
knitr::kable(cache$start[, .(model, n_par, fmt(objective, 3), sci(max_abs_gradient, 2))],
             col.names = c("Configuration", "Estimated parameters", "Objective", "Max |gradient|"),
             align = "lrrr")
```

The objective must be finite. At the converted SS3 optimum, the gradient is
not zero, because the two models' likelihoods differ, but it should not be
huge. A very large gradient on one parameter usually means a scale error in
that parameter or in the data it fits.

# Set up and fit the final model

The bridging configuration used SS3's selectivity as fixed data. The final
model, C2, uses opal's own length-based selectivity curves instead, with the
opal equivalent of each parameter SS3 estimated being estimated here too.

## Seed opal's selectivity from SS3's

SS3's selectivity here is on age, while opal's is on length, and there is no
algebraic conversion between the two. `ss3_seed_par_sel()` projects SS3's
selectivity-at-age onto the length bins using SS3's age–length key. It then
fits each opal curve to that projection by least squares, using opal's own
selectivity functions so that the seeded values are on opal's scale.

```{r seed-selectivity}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
```

```{r seed-table}
sr = cache$seed_rmse[, .(fishery = as.character(fleet_name(fishery)),
                         curve = c("logistic", "double-normal", "double Richards")[sel_type],
                         rmse = fmt(rmse, 3))]
knitr::kable(sr, col.names = c("Fishery", "opal curve", "RMSE against SS3"), align = "llr")
```

The RMSE is on the selectivity scale (0–1) and shows how well the chosen
opal curve can follow SS3's shape. A large value for a fishery means that
curve family does not fit SS3's shape, so change `opal_type_f` for that
fishery before fitting.

## Choose what to estimate

`ss3_use_estimated_selectivity()` removes SS3's selectivity from the model,
puts in the seeded curves and writes the selectivity part of the map from
`cfg$selectivity`:

* **`estimate`**: fisheries whose curves are estimated. IO YFT: the 14
  fishing fleets with their own selectivity in SS3, and the index.
* **`free_par`**: which curve parameters are estimated, by opal curve family.
  For the double-normal, columns 1–4 (peak, top width, ascending and
  descending widths) are estimated, as SS3 estimated P1–P4 of its pattern
  20. For the logistic, both parameters are estimated.
* **`mirror`**: fisheries sharing another fishery's parameters (SS3 pattern
  15). Fisheries 15 and 16 mirror 14; the four quarterly index series share
  one curve.
* **`fix`**: parameters held at their seeded values. In an earlier fit
  (C), these nine went to the mean of opal's selectivity prior, which
  meant the length data did not inform them, so C2 fixes them.

```{r final-model}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
```

```{r estimated-table}
knitr::kable(cache$estimated, col.names = c("Parameter", "Estimated"))
```

The `r sum(cache$estimated$n_estimated)` estimated parameters are `log_B0`,
the `r cache$estimated[parameter == "rdev_y", n_estimated]` recruitment
deviations, the four catchabilities and
`r cache$estimated[parameter == "par_sel", n_estimated]` selectivity
parameters. Growth, steepness, σ~R~ and the observation variances stay at
their SS3 or default values (opal's default map).

## Fit

```{r fit}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
```

`opal_fit()` runs `nlminb` (here two passes). `nlminb` stops on relative
change in the objective, which for an objective of this size can leave
gradients near 10^-3^. `ss3_newton_polish()` then takes a few Newton steps
with the exact RTMB Hessian. `opal_attach_fit()` puts the polished optimum
back on the object and runs `opal_check()`, which checks the gradient (here
to 10^-4^), that the Hessian is positive definite and that the parameters
are estimable.

```{r convergence-table}
#| tbl-colwidths: [14, 14, 14, 10, 18, 16, 14]
knitr::kable(C[, .(fmt(objective_start, 2), fmt(objective_fit, 3), sci(max_gradient, 1),
                   newton_steps, ifelse(positive_hessian, "yes", "**no**"),
                   ifelse(check_passes, "passed", "**failed**"), fmt(seconds, 0))],
             col.names = c("Objective at start", "Objective at fit", "Max |gradient|",
                           "Newton steps", "Positive definite Hessian", "opal_check()",
                           "Seconds"),
             align = "rrrrccr")
```

## Save

```{r save}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
```

`opal_save()` stores the whole object: data, parameters, map, fit and
provenance. `opal_read(path, rebuild = TRUE)` loads it again and rebuilds the
RTMB tape, ready for `opal_report()`.

# A first look at the fit

These figures only check that the fitted model is sensible and close to
SS3. The two vignettes listed in section 1 have the full comparison, including
against the simulated truth. The companion script's `results` chunk builds
these tables from `opal_report(fit)` and SS3's `Report.sso`, and can be
reused as it is.

```{r index-figure}
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Longline index, each quarterly series scaled to mean 1: observations (points, ±1.96 SE), opal's fit and SS3's expected values."
ci = cache$cpue
ci[, series := fleet_name(fishery)]
cl = rbind(ci[, .(ts, series, value = opal, model = "opal")],
           ci[, .(ts, series, value = ss3,  model = "SS3")])
ggplot() +
    geom_pointrange(data = ci, aes(ts, obs, ymin = obs * exp(-1.96 * se), ymax = obs * exp(1.96 * se)),
                    colour = "grey60", size = 0.15, linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_line(data = cl, aes(ts, value, colour = model), linewidth = 0.6) +
    facet_wrap(~series, ncol = 2) +
    scale_series + labs(x = "Time step (quarter)", y = "Index (mean 1)")
```

```{r lf-figure}
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Length compositions aggregated over all observations for each fishery, weighted by sample size: observed (bars), opal's and SS3's expected."
lf = cache$lf
lf[, series := fleet_name(fishery)]
ll = rbind(lf[, .(series, bin, value = opal, model = "opal")],
           lf[, .(series, bin, value = ss3,  model = "SS3")])
ggplot() +
    geom_col(data = lf, aes(bin + 2.5, obs), fill = "grey85", width = 5) +
    geom_line(data = ll, aes(bin + 2.5, value, colour = model), linewidth = 0.5) +
    facet_wrap(~series, ncol = 4, scales = "free_y") +
    scale_series + labs(x = "Length (cm)", y = "Proportion") +
    theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 8), axis.text.y = element_blank(),
          axis.ticks.y = element_blank())
```

```{r sel-figure}
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Selectivity-at-age: SS3's (age-based) and opal's fitted length-based curves mapped to age through the age–length key. Fisheries 15, 16 and 18–20 are mirrors and are not shown."
sl = cache$selectivity[fishery %in% c(1:14, 17)]
sl[, series := fleet_name(fishery)]
ggplot(sl, aes(age, sel, colour = model)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
    facet_wrap(~series, ncol = 4) +
    scale_series + labs(x = "Age (quarters)", y = "Selectivity") +
    theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 8))
```

```{r ssb-figure}
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Spawning biomass (top) and spawning biomass relative to B0 (bottom): SS3 and the fitted opal model."
tl = rbind(cache$trajectory[, .(ts, model, value = ssb, panel = "Spawning biomass (t)")],
           cache$trajectory[, .(ts, model, value = depletion, panel = "SSB / B0")])
ggplot(tl, aes(ts, value, colour = model)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
    facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
    expand_limits(y = 0) +
    scale_series + labs(x = "Time step (quarter)", y = NULL)
```

```{r summary-table}
st = S[, .(quantity,
           SS3  = ifelse(quantity == "Terminal SSB / B0", fmt(SS3, 3), fmt(SS3, 0)),
           opal = ifelse(quantity == "Terminal SSB / B0", fmt(opal, 3), fmt(opal, 0)),
           ratio = fmt(opal / SS3, 2))]
knitr::kable(st, col.names = c("Quantity", "SS3", "opal", "opal / SS3"), align = "lrrr")
```

For IO YFT, opal's B0 is `r fmt(S[1, opal / SS3], 2)` × SS3's, and its
terminal SSB/B0 is `r fmt(S[3, opal], 2)` against SS3's `r fmt(S[3, SS3], 2)`.
Most of that gap comes from selectivity. When the same opal model is fitted
with SS3's selectivity-at-age held fixed (fit A1 in
`ss3-to-opal-io-yft-age-k.qmd`), its terminal SSB/B0 is within 0.01 of SS3's.
The remaining sources of difference are:

* catch timing;
* opal's length-based selectivity curves, which cannot match every SS3
  age-based shape;
* the index split into four series with separate catchabilities;
* SS3 data that opal does not use (here, the survey's generalised size
  compositions).

What matters is that the gap can be explained. The two vignettes explain the
IO YFT gap one cause at a time.

# From yellowfin to your model

The converter was written for, and tested on, this one SS3 model. It reads
the general SS3 file layout through r4ss, but wherever IO YFT did not need a
feature, the code does not handle it. Before converting another model, list
its features with `ss3_model_features()` and compare them with IO YFT's. Each
difference tells you which function to check or extend. The last column
points to where to start.

```{r features-table}
#| tbl-colwidths: [20, 13, 13, 54]
notes = c(
    "SS3 version" = "Tested on 3.24 only. `ss3_read_model()` reads the par file with `SS_readpar_3.24()`, and `ss3_lencomp_n_mult()` and the catch row of `ss3_reconcile()` expect 3.24 layouts. For 3.30, check every reader in `ss3-convert.R`, and `ss3_recdevs()`.",
    "Model period (SS3 years)" = "`cfg$time`; the opal step is the SS3 year.",
    "Seasons per year" = "The converter assumes `nseas = 1`: opal gets `n_season = 1`, and `ss3_catch_to_opal()` keeps one catch value per year and fleet.",
    "Months per season" = "Sets the M and K divisor (`ss3_m_rate_divisor()`).",
    "Sexes" = "Single-sex only. `ss3_endgrowth_table()` keeps the first sex; two-sex compositions and spawning output need new code.",
    "Areas" = "Single area only.",
    "Ages (max)" = "`cfg$age`.",
    "Fishing fleets" = "One opal fishery per SS3 fleet, in SS3 order.",
    "Survey / index fleets" = "`cfg$index` (`keep_ss3_fleets`, `split`); opal adds one fishery per index series.",
    "Catch units (1 biomass, 2 numbers)" = "Passed through (opal uses the same codes).",
    "Index observations" = "`ss3_index_to_opal()`; negative fleet codes are dropped; scaled to mean 1.",
    "Length composition rows" = "`ss3_lencomp_to_opal()`; one sex, no partitions. `mult_by_lencomp_N` becomes `lf_var_adjust`.",
    "Age composition rows" = "Not converted. Conditional age-at-length or age data need new code.",
    "Generalised size comp methods" = "Not converted (IO YFT's survey size data are dropped).",
    "Tag release groups" = "Not converted.",
    "Growth model (1 vB, 2 Richards, 3 age-K)" = "3: `growth$model = \"ss3_age_k\"` (exact). 1: `\"schnute\"`, which matches von Bertalanffy. 2: Schnute approximation only; check the length-at-age row of `ss3_reconcile()`.",
    "Growth patterns" = "One expected.",
    "Platoons per growth pattern" = "One expected. With platoons, `ss3_endgrowth_table()` averages rows without abundance weights and warns.",
    "Length selectivity patterns" = "Any pattern works for the bridging test (selectivity is read from `ageselex`). For the final model, choose `opal_type_f` to suit SS3's shapes and check the seeding RMSE.",
    "Age selectivity patterns" = "As above.",
    "Time-block designs" = "Only one year of selectivity is used (`selectivity$reference_year`). Time-varying selectivity is not represented.",
    "F method" = "opal removes catch at the start of each step; the bridging test measures the effect.",
    "Stock-recruit function" = "opal is Beverton–Holt; steepness and σR are read from the par file.",
    "Report.sso available" = "Required for the `endgrowth` route, selectivity, B0 and the bridging test.")
ft = cache$features[, .(feature, yft = value, yours = " ", where = notes[feature])]
# Shorten SS3's full version banner to its number.
ft[feature == "SS3 version", yft := sub("^SS-V([0-9.]+[A-Za-z]*).*", "\\1", yft)]
knitr::kable(ft, col.names = c("Feature", "IO YFT", "Your model", "What the converter does / where to look"))
```

The converter also assumes the following, which are not in the table:

* **Initial conditions.** The converter starts the population unfished:
  initial F is effectively zero and there are no initial age deviations. If
  your model starts from a fished equilibrium (initial equilibrium catch or
  initial F), `ss3_pars_to_opal()` has to set `log_init_F_f` and the map has
  to estimate it.
* **Recruitment deviations.** Early and main deviations are read from the par
  file (`ss3_recdevs()`), and SS3's bias-adjustment ramp from Report.sso.
  Forecast deviations are ignored.
* **Parameters with environmental links, time variation or deviations**
  (other than recruitment) are not converted. Their effects on selectivity
  and biology are captured only through the single reference year read from
  Report.sso.

A suggested order for a new model:

1. Run `ss3_model_features()` and fill in the "Your model" column.
2. Set up `cfg` and get `ss3_to_opal()` to run, extending the converter
   where the table says it needs to.
3. Make tests 1 and 2 pass exactly before anything else.
4. Run the bridging test and make the replay with SS3 timing match SS3.
5. Only then set up the opal selectivity and fit.

The SS3 model used here (`case-studies/io-yft/model-files/ss3/xx-io-yft-sim-iattc-sample-tree-4`)
was developed by the IATTC analyst team for the Spatial Stock Assessment
Simulation Experiment: Mark N. Maunder, Haikun Xu and Carolina Minte-Vera
(Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission). The yellowfin assessments from the
experiment, including theirs, are evaluated in Goethel, D.R., et al. (2024).
'Drivin' with your eyes closed': Results from an international, blinded
simulation experiment to evaluate spatial stock assessments. *Fish and
Fisheries* 25(3): 471–490. <https://doi.org/10.1111/faf.12819>
